country.comment: Case study of the peripheral neighborhood of Mesa Colorada in the municipality of Zapopan, state of Jalisco, Mexico (Guadalajara Metropolitan Area).
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Resumen & Abstract; PDF p. 4, Section 'Guadalajara y su zona metropolitana'; PDF p. 5, Mapa 1

effect_estimate.comment: Qualitative historical-environmental case study with descriptive contextual figures (e.g., ~19,887–20,000 residents across 2,200 homes; Agua Prieta plant capacity 6,500 L/s; vended water expenses exceeding 10% of household income in some cases) and no inferential numeric effect estimate.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Irregular ejido land subdivisions and costly, protracted regularization/titling processes (CORET 1998–2008, with many homes still unregularized in 2025) were used for years by the municipal government to justify withholding basic public services including piped water and continue to exclude households lacking possession documents from housing programs; simultaneously, state and metropolitan governance (SIAPA) sited the Agua Prieta wastewater treatment plant (6,500 L/s capacity) adjacent to Mesa Colorada as a peripheral 'sacrifice zone' while leaving residents with limited, intermittent water supply despite installed infrastructure, tariff billing, and Mexico's 2012 constitutional human right to water (Art. 4), forcing households to buy vended water costing over 10% of income in some cases and reuse household greywater multiple times.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF pp. 1–2, Resumen & Abstract; PDF pp. 5–6, Section 'Guadalajara y su zona metropolitana'; PDF pp. 7–12, Section 1; PDF pp. 14–16, Section 2; PDF pp. 17–18, Conclusiones

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at 2 by the qualitative design ceiling (CODEBOOK.md §9). Rated 2 because primary archival press records and resident interviews directly document the legal/administrative mechanisms affecting water access: municipal refusal to provide basic services justified by unregularized ejido land sales, slow and costly titling/regularization (CORET/SRA) leaving families without possession documents, and metropolitan planning/SIAPA service allocation prioritizing central Guadalajara while leaving peripheral Mesa Colorada with intermittent supply despite installed pipes and tariff payments.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 5–6, Section 'Guadalajara y su zona metropolitana'; PDF pp. 7–9 & 12, Section 1

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines irregular ejido land tenure used by municipal authorities to justify withholding basic public services (ELIGIBILITY: tenure), lack of possession/title documentation excluding families from social housing programs (documentation), urban land-use/megaproject planning and metropolitan SIAPA water allocation across central vs. peripheral areas (planning, service_area), costly deeding/regularization processes plus monthly tariffs and high vended water costs (BURDEN: fees), and multi-year delays in land regularization and municipal response to neighborhood water demands (delay).
mechanism_flags.value: ELIGIBILITY, BURDEN, tenure, documentation, planning, service_area, fees, delay
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 5–6, Section 'Guadalajara y su zona metropolitana'; PDF pp. 7–9 & 12, Section 1; PDF pp. 17–18, Conclusiones

outcome_flags.comment: Analyzes household lack of safe and sufficient drinking water (water_access, service_quantity), initial lack and later regularization of drainage alongside local exposure to metropolitan wastewater treatment (sanitation_access), limited and intermittent piped water delivery despite installed infrastructure (service_continuity), and monthly tariffs paired with vended water expenditures exceeding 10% of family income in some cases (affordability).

study_design.value: Qualitative historical-environmental case study (open-ended semi-structured interviews, home visits and field observation, and coded triangulation with local newspaper archives and census data)
